newsitem.title: UK: IRA truce hopes raised after splinter group bomb.
newsitem.headline: IRA truce hopes raised after splinter group bomb.

text.p: A Northern Irish Catholic leader said the Irish Republican Army was willing to call a new truce, hours after a republican splinter group planted a huge car bomb in Londonderry.

The 600-lb (250-kg) placed outside police headquarters in a heavily populated part of the city was defused before it could explode, but the attack threatened to disrupt Northern Ireland's faltering peace process.
Security analysts said the emergence of the Irish Continuity Army Council (CAC), which claimed responsibilty for planting the bomb, was a dangerous twist in the delicate search for peace.
The group is said to have broken away from the IRA ten years ago in protest at a peace strategy advocated by the IRA's political wing Sinn Fein.

But while the latest attack appeared to undermine peace efforts, Social Democratic and Labour Party leader John Hume said he believed the IRA was ready to renew the ceasefire it abandoned in February if Britain agreed to proposals he put forward.
Media reports said Hume had urged Britain to set a rigid timetable for the all-party peace talks on the future of Northern Ireland.
In exchange, the IRA would call a new truce so that Sinn Fein could be granted a seat at the talks table.
"I will put my head on the line for this. I am absolutely convinced now we can achieve an absolutely genuine, unequivocal restoration (of the ceasefire)," Hume told the BBC.
Britain and Ireland have said Sinn Fein will not be allowed into talks until the IRA declares a full ceasefire.
Sinn Fein says it wants an unconditional seat at the talks if the IRA does adopt a new truce in its war to end British rule of Northern Ireland.
Pro-British "loyalist" politicians have been allowed into the talks because their guerrilla allies are still honouring ceasefires they called two years ago to match the IRA's now defunct one.
Hume has been holding talks with Sinn Fein leader Gerry Adams and with British and Irish leaders to try to get a new IRA ceasefire and breathe new life into the peace process.
Britain and Sinn Fein have both denied an Irish newspaper report suggesting that the IRA was operating an unofficial ceasefire to get Sinn Fein into the talks.
British Prime Minister John Major on Thursday met Protestant leaders in London and once more stressed to them he was not doing any "back door deals" with Sinn Fein.
Hume appealed to Loyalist guerrillas not to retaliate to the Londonderry bomb, and called the the CAC "enemies of all the people of Ireland".
Protestant politicians said they believed the IRA was involved.
"Anything happening there (Northern Ireland) in terms of republican violence will have the blessing of the Provisional IRA," said Ulster Unionist Party spokesman Ken Maginnis.
Sinn Fein said the incident underlined the urgent need for a negotiated Northern Ireland settlement.

"It shows the need for all those interested in peace to redouble their efforts to remove all preconditions and obstacles to a truly meaningful peace process," said Gerry O'Hara, chairman of Sinn Fein in Northern Ireland.
